title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation modulates auditory-evoked responses and conflict adaptation in humans
byline: Kamatani; Issey; Kabe; Yasuo; Kumagai; Shinichi; Onuki; Yoshiyuki; Xu; Hexin; Shiramatsu; Tomoyo Isoguchi; Kunii; Naoto; Kawai; Kensuke; Takahashi; Hirokazu
html:
Abstract:Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) engages ascending neuromodulatory systems, and animal studies have motivated the hypothesis that it shifts sensory cortical processing toward feedforward (FF) relative to feedback (FB) transmission. Whether transcutaneous auricular VNS (taVNS) produces a corresponding pattern in humans remains unclear. In a single-blind, sham-controlled crossover study, 11 healthy adults received 120 min of taVNS (25 Hz, left tragus) and sham stimulation (left earlobe) in separate sessions. Click-evoked EEG was recorded before, twice during, and immediately after stimulation. Sensory discrimination thresholds and conflict adaptation in a Simon task were assessed before and during stimulation. Relative to Sham, taVNS attenuated the decline in the early P0 response across the session and enhanced the Pa-Nb response early during stimulation. The later P2 response did not show the increase observed under Sham. After stimulation, taVNS reduced click-locked theta (5-8 Hz) inter-trial phase coherence relative to Sham, with no significant between-condition difference in the change in theta power. Conflict adaptation increased under taVNS, whereas sensory thresholds and the overall Simon effect did not differ significantly between conditions. In exploratory analysis, greater decreases in theta phase coherence were associated with greater increases in conflict adaptation. These findings indicate that taVNS modulates auditory responses across processing stages and conflict-related behavior. The pattern is compatible with altered FF/FB weighting, but the direction of information flow and the underlying neuromodulatory mechanisms were not measured directly.
